It differs from wide-interval weighting (uniformly 1) by covering only the minimal interval widths needed to cover non-transparent portions of color-opacity transfer functions, yielding results closer to ground truth [S2].

The claim states that narrow-interval weighting differs from wide-interval weighting (uniformly 1) by covering only the minimal interval widths needed to cover non-transparent portions of color-opacity transfer functions, yielding results closer to ground truth. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in Section 4.3, stating: 'Narrow interval widths are the minimal interval widths needed to cover the non-transparent portions of the color-opacity transfer functions used for producing the figures, while wide interval widths cover the entire value domain.' It further states that 'choosing narrow, salient intervals... yields improved quality' and that the narrower interval 'clearly yields a result closer to the ground truth than the wide interval of interest'.
supported

All variables ($x$, $c$, $w$, $C$) and their definitions in the claim match those in the source.

Unlike [Colormap Application for Visualization](7714-colormap-application-for-visualization.md), which maps the entire domain to a spectrum, or [Clamping](11530-clamping.md), which maps out-of-range values to the boundary colors of the transfer function, windowing explicitly discards out-of-range information into neutral background colors [S1, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines windowing as a transfer function that maps a specific range of data values (the 'window') to a linear ramp of grayscales, while mapping values outside this range to black or white. Black and white are neutral background colors. This directly supports the claim that windowing explicitly discards out-of-range information into neutral background colors.
supported

It solves the problem of low contrast in volumetric data by isolating a "window" of interest (e.g., soft tissue) from the full data range, preventing background noise or irrelevant high-intensity structures (e.g., bone) from obscuring the target features [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that windowing maps a specific range of data values ('window') to a linear ramp of grayscales, while values outside this range are mapped to black or white. The passage regarding histograms illustrates how a 'Tissue Window' can be used to isolate specific constituents (like tissue) from others (like bone) present in the full data range. This aligns with the claim's description of isolating a window of interest to prevent irrelevant structures from obscuring target features.
